templates.title: The plan that stopped using the index
templates.prompt: Read the query plan and say what is actually wrong. Restating the symptom does not count.
templates.objective: Read a query plan and connect a sequential scan to a missing index.
hints: Look at what the filter is on, then at what the indexes cover.
Note how many rows were read compared with how many were returned.
templates.explanation: Seq Scan plus a large Rows Removed by Filter is the signature of a missing index: the database is reading everything and throwing nearly all of it away. The existing indexes cover the primary key and created_at, neither of which the filter uses. The query did not change — the table grew until the scan became expensive.

answerKey.body:
Seq Scan on orders  (cost=0.00..48210.00 rows=1200000 width=84)
  Filter: ((user_id = 42) AND (status = 'OPEN'::text))
  Rows Removed by Filter: 1199987
Planning Time: 0.21 ms
Execution Time: 843.55 ms

Indexes on orders:
  orders_pkey            PRIMARY KEY (id)
  orders_created_at_idx  btree (created_at)
answerKey.symptom: This endpoint was 40ms last month. It is 900ms now, and nothing about the query changed.
answerKey.rootCause: There is no index on the columns being filtered, so the database scans all 1.2 million rows and discards 99.999% of them.
acceptableFixes: Add a composite index on (user_id, status)
Add an index on user_id, the more selective of the two columns

goodAnswerSignals: Names the missing index on the filtered columns
Reads Seq Scan and Rows Removed as the evidence
weakAnswerSignals: Says the query is slow because the table is large
Suggests more memory or a bigger instance
followUpPrompts: Which column order would you use in the composite index?
mayaPushbacks: What are the existing indexes actually covering?

templates.title: Sorted in memory
templates.prompt: Read the query plan and explain what is causing the slowdown.
templates.objective: Recognize a sort that spills to disk because the index covers the filter but not the ordering.
hints: Compare the row count entering the Sort with the row count leaving the Limit.
Sort Method names where the sort happened.
templates.explanation: The Index Scan does its job — it finds the post's comments. But Sort Method: external merge with 68MB on disk shows the database then ordered a quarter of a million rows in temporary files to return twenty. An index whose columns match filter then sort order lets it walk in output order and stop at the limit.

answerKey.body:
Limit  (cost=41200.10..41200.15 rows=20 width=120)
  ->  Sort  (cost=41200.10..41880.42 rows=272128 width=120)
        Sort Key: created_at DESC
        Sort Method: external merge  Disk: 68400kB
        ->  Index Scan using comments_post_id_idx on comments
              (cost=0.43..9820.55 rows=272128 width=120)
              Index Cond: (post_id = 91)
Execution Time: 1187.90 ms
answerKey.symptom: A list endpoint returns 20 rows but takes 1.2 seconds for large accounts.
answerKey.rootCause: The index narrows to the post but does not provide the ordering, so 272,128 rows are sorted on disk before 20 are returned.
acceptableFixes: Add a composite index on (post_id, created_at DESC) so the index supplies the order
Use keyset pagination on created_at so the index can seek and stop

goodAnswerSignals: Connects the disk sort to an index that lacks the sort column
Proposes a composite index in sort order
weakAnswerSignals: Says the index is missing entirely
Suggests raising work_mem and stopping there
followUpPrompts: Why does the column order in the composite index matter here?
mayaPushbacks: The index scan is being used — so what is slow?

templates.title: Fast query, slow endpoint
templates.prompt: The database says every query is fast. The endpoint is not. Explain what the log shows.
templates.objective: Recognize an N+1 from a request log rather than from source code.
hints: Count the statements and compare that with the LIMIT on the first one.
Ask why nothing appeared in the slow query log.
templates.explanation: No individual statement is slow enough to reach the slow query log, which is why it looked empty. The repetition is the signal: the same statement fifty times, once per row from the first query. Round trip overhead dominates, and the fix is to make the query count constant rather than to make each query faster.

answerKey.body:
[db] SELECT * FROM posts ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 50   3.1ms
[db] SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1                       0.9ms
[db] SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1                       0.8ms
[db] SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1                       1.1ms
[db] SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = $1                       0.9ms
... 46 more identical statements ...
[req] GET /api/posts                                      1402ms
answerKey.symptom: The p99 for GET /api/posts is 1.4s, but the slow query log is empty.
answerKey.rootCause: The endpoint issues one query per row returned — an N+1 — so 51 individually fast queries add up to a slow request.
acceptableFixes: Join the author in the original query
Collect the author ids and fetch them in a single batched query

goodAnswerSignals: Names the N+1 from the repetition
Explains why per-query timing hid it
weakAnswerSignals: Suggests caching without naming the pattern
followUpPrompts: Why did the slow query log not catch this?
mayaPushbacks: Is any single query here slow?

templates.title: Waiting on the pool
templates.prompt: Read the metrics and explain what is causing the errors.
templates.objective: Separate a database problem from a resource-holding problem that looks like one.
hints: Compare the query duration with the acquire time.
Look for something in the metrics that takes seconds rather than milliseconds.
templates.explanation: Query duration is 11ms — the database is healthy. But every one of the 20 connections is in use and 96 requests are queued. The external API at 8.4s is the clue: connections are being held across that call. The fix is to stop holding a pooled resource while waiting on something you do not control.

answerKey.body:
db.pool.size                  20
db.pool.in_use                20
db.pool.waiting               96
db.pool.acquire_p99         30s   (timeout)
db.query.duration_p99       11ms

http.requests_in_flight      116
http.request_duration_p99   30s
external.report_api.p99     8.4s
answerKey.symptom: Requests started failing with 'timeout acquiring connection' during a traffic spike.
answerKey.rootCause: Connections are held while waiting on a slow external call, so the pool is exhausted even though the database itself is fast.
acceptableFixes: Move the external call outside the connection or transaction scope
Release the connection before calling the external service and reacquire afterwards
Add a timeout to the external call so connections are not held for 8 seconds

goodAnswerSignals: Notices the database is fast while the pool is starved
Connects the external call to connection holding
weakAnswerSignals: Says the pool is simply too small
Blames the database for the timeouts
followUpPrompts: Would raising the pool size fix this or delay it?
mayaPushbacks: Is the database actually slow here?

templates.title: The chain in the waterfall
templates.prompt: Read the waterfall and explain why the page is slow to render.
templates.objective: Read a waterfall and identify serialization rather than slowness.
hints: Look at where each bar starts relative to the previous one.
Add up the durations, then ask which of them actually depend on each other.
templates.explanation: No individual request is slow — the longest is 490ms. The problem is the staircase: each bar starts exactly where the previous ends, so latency is the sum rather than the maximum. Three of the four data requests do not depend on each other and could run together.

answerKey.body:
index.html            |=====|                              0ms   120ms
app.js                      |=========|                    120ms  610ms
config.json                            |=====|             610ms  790ms
user.json                                    |======|      790ms 1040ms
prefs.json                                          |====| 1040ms 1250ms
dashboard.json                                           |=======| 1250ms 1680ms
[render]                                                          1680ms
answerKey.symptom: First contentful paint is 3.4s on a fast connection.
answerKey.rootCause: Each request only starts when the previous one finishes — a request chain, where every response is required before the next request is issued.
acceptableFixes: Fetch config, user and prefs concurrently once app.js loads
Preload or inline the configuration so the chain starts shorter
Return the four payloads from a single endpoint

goodAnswerSignals: Names the request chain
Identifies which requests could run concurrently
followUpPrompts: Which of these four genuinely depends on another?
mayaPushbacks: Is any single request here slow?

templates.title: Cached, and yet not
templates.prompt: Read the response headers and explain why the cache is not helping.
templates.objective: Recognize a cache key that fragments to one entry per user.
hints: Ask what the CDN uses as the cache key here.
Notice that the response both sets a cookie and varies on one.
templates.explanation: max-age looks correct in isolation, but Vary: Cookie makes the cookie part of the cache key. Because every visitor has a distinct session hint — set by this very response — no two requests share a key. A 0.4% hit ratio is what a fragmented key looks like.

answerKey.body:
GET /api/catalog
< HTTP/1.1 200 OK
< Cache-Control: max-age=300
< Set-Cookie: session_hint=a91f; Path=/
< Vary: Cookie
< Content-Length: 184203

CDN report:
  hit ratio          0.4%
  origin requests    98,220 / day
answerKey.symptom: A CDN was added in front of the API but the origin traffic did not drop.
answerKey.rootCause: The response varies on Cookie and sets a cookie, so the CDN caches a separate entry per unique cookie value and effectively never gets a hit.
acceptableFixes: Remove Vary: Cookie from responses that do not depend on the cookie
Stop setting a cookie on this cacheable endpoint
Serve the catalog from a cookieless path or subdomain

goodAnswerSignals: Names Vary: Cookie fragmenting the key
Connects the Set-Cookie to the fragmentation
followUpPrompts: Which of these two headers would you remove first?
mayaPushbacks: How many distinct cache entries does this produce?

templates.title: Retry, meet outage
templates.prompt: Read the metrics and explain what turned a partial failure into a total one.
templates.objective: Connect a retry policy to load amplification during a degradation.
hints: Compare the request rate before and during the incident.
Ask why a restart did not restore service.
templates.explanation: Request rate goes from 420 to 3980 while nothing upstream asked for more traffic — that increase is retries. Each failure became four attempts, so the dependency received more load precisely as it became less able to serve it. The restart did not help because the retry storm resumed instantly.

answerKey.body:
14:00  payments.rps   420    error_rate 0.1%   p99  180ms
14:02  payments.rps   445    error_rate 8.0%   p99  2.1s
14:03  payments.rps  1310    error_rate 42%    p99  9.8s
14:05  payments.rps  3980    error_rate 97%    p99  timeout
14:12  payments.rps  3860    error_rate 99%    (after restart)

client retry policy: 3 attempts, no delay
answerKey.symptom: A dependency degraded at 14:02. By 14:05 it was completely down and stayed down after it was restarted.
answerKey.rootCause: Immediate retries multiplied request volume exactly as the dependency degraded, so client load grew roughly fourfold and prevented any recovery.
acceptableFixes: Add exponential backoff with jitter to the retry policy
Add a circuit breaker so clients stop calling a failing dependency
Cap total retry budget across clients rather than per request

goodAnswerSignals: Names retry amplification
Explains why the restart failed to recover
weakAnswerSignals: Says the dependency was simply undersized
followUpPrompts: Why does a circuit breaker help where backoff alone might not?
mayaPushbacks: What caused the request rate to grow nine times?

templates.title: The leak with a sawtooth
templates.prompt: Read the memory series and explain what it shows.
templates.objective: Distinguish a memory leak from ordinary load-driven memory use.
hints: Note that traffic is flat while memory is not.
Watch what happens to GC frequency as the heap grows.
templates.explanation: Traffic is flat, so this is not load. Heap climbs steadily and major GC frequency rises with it — the collector is working harder and reclaiming less, which means the objects are still referenced. The reset at 14:00 is the restart, not a recovery. Something is retaining objects across requests.

answerKey.symptom: The service restarts itself every few hours. CPU and traffic are flat.
answerKey.rootCause: Heap grows monotonically and is never reclaimed, so something retains references across requests until the process is killed.
acceptableFixes: Find and bound the growing structure — usually a cache or registry with no eviction
Add a TTL or size limit to whatever accumulates per request
Remove listeners or subscriptions that are registered but never released

goodAnswerSignals: Names retained references rather than load
Reads rising GC with rising heap as failure to reclaim
weakAnswerSignals: Says the service needs more memory
followUpPrompts: What would this graph look like if it were load rather than a leak?
mayaPushbacks: Is the collector failing to run, or failing to free?

templates.title: Locked behind each other
templates.prompt: Read the log and explain why throughput collapsed.
templates.objective: Connect lock contention to transaction scope rather than to database load.
hints: Compare the statement durations with the total transaction duration.
Ask what is holding the inventory row lock for that long.
templates.explanation: CPU is low and the individual statements take milliseconds — the database is not busy, it is waiting. The transaction stays open for 1851ms because of a network call in the middle, and the inventory row lock is held that whole time. Every other order for that SKU serializes behind it.

answerKey.body:
[tx 8812] BEGIN
[tx 8812] UPDATE inventory SET count = count - 1 WHERE sku = 'A1'   2ms
[tx 8812] POST https://fulfilment.example.com/reserve            1840ms
[tx 8812] INSERT INTO orders ...                                    3ms
[tx 8812] COMMIT                                       total: 1851ms

pg_locks: 47 waiting on relation "inventory" row (sku='A1')
lock_wait_p99: 6.4s
answerKey.symptom: Order creation throughput dropped from 300/min to 20/min. CPU is under 15%.
answerKey.rootCause: An external HTTP call runs inside the transaction, so the row lock on the popular SKU is held for nearly two seconds per order and every other order queues behind it.
acceptableFixes: Move the fulfilment call outside the transaction
Reserve inventory in a short transaction, then call fulfilment, then commit the order separately
Restructure so the lock is held only for the database writes

goodAnswerSignals: Names the external call inside the transaction
Connects lock hold time to throughput collapse
weakAnswerSignals: Says the database needs more connections
followUpPrompts: What breaks if you simply move the call after COMMIT?
mayaPushbacks: Why is CPU low if the database is the bottleneck?

templates.title: Deployed at 14:20
templates.prompt: Read the series and say what the evidence supports as the cause.
templates.objective: Read a time series well enough to reject a plausible but unsupported explanation.
hints: Check whether the request rate actually grew.
Look at what happens to the error rate when traffic falls at 15:10.
templates.explanation: Request rate never rises — it is flat and then falls. The error rate steps at the deploy boundary and stays high even when traffic drops by a third, which is the opposite of what load-driven failure looks like. The 15:10 row is the decisive one: fewer requests, same error rate.

answerKey.symptom: Error rate rose in the afternoon. Someone suggested it is because traffic grew.
answerKey.rootCause: Traffic is flat throughout and errors begin immediately after the v412 deploy, so the release is the cause rather than load.
acceptableFixes: Roll back v412 and confirm the error rate returns to baseline
Bisect the changes in v412 against the failing endpoint

goodAnswerSignals: Rejects the load explanation using the 15:10 row
Ties the step change to the deploy
weakAnswerSignals: Says more investigation is needed without reading the series
followUpPrompts: What would you expect to see if this really were load?

templates.title: Slow for some people only
templates.prompt: Read the breakdown and explain what it points to.
templates.objective: Read a bucketed distribution and identify unbounded work per request.
hints: Look at how p99 changes across the account size buckets.
Note how many rows a single request can return.
templates.explanation: The p50 is healthy, which is why most users are fine. The bucketing shows latency tracking account size almost linearly, and rows_returned at 41,900 confirms the endpoint has no upper bound on how much it does. Aggregate percentiles hid this; the breakdown reveals it.

answerKey.body:
endpoint /api/feed
  p50    120ms
  p90    140ms
  p99   4900ms

by account_size bucket:
  <100 items      p99   130ms
  100-1k items    p99   180ms
  1k-10k items    p99  1900ms
  >10k items      p99  9200ms

rows_returned p99: 41,900
answerKey.symptom: Most users report the app is fast. A minority say it is unusable.
answerKey.rootCause: Latency scales with account size because the endpoint returns every item instead of a bounded page, so large accounts get proportionally slower.
acceptableFixes: Paginate the endpoint with a bounded page size
Push filtering and a limit into the query rather than returning everything

goodAnswerSignals: Ties latency to unbounded result size
Uses the bucketing rather than the aggregate
followUpPrompts: Why did the aggregate p99 make this hard to spot?
mayaPushbacks: What bounds how much work one request does?

templates.title: Duplicated at the boundary
templates.prompt: Read the log and explain how the customer was charged twice.
templates.objective: Recognize that a timeout is an ambiguous outcome, not a failure.
hints: Compare the gateway's timestamp for ch_7740 with our timeout.
Note what the idem_key field says on both attempts.
templates.explanation: The gateway statement shows ch_7740 succeeding 90ms before our client gave up — the payment worked, the response did not arrive. Because attempt=2 carried no idempotency key, the gateway had no way to recognize it as the same payment. Our logs show one order because only the second charge was recorded.

answerKey.body:
14:22:01.114  POST /api/checkout        request_id=r-88a1
14:22:01.180  gateway.charge  attempt=1  idem_key=absent
14:22:11.180  gateway.charge  attempt=1  TIMEOUT after 10000ms
14:22:11.181  gateway.charge  attempt=2  idem_key=absent
14:22:12.402  gateway.charge  attempt=2  OK  txn=ch_7741
14:22:12.410  orders.create   order=o-3391  txn=ch_7741

gateway statement:
  ch_7740  succeeded  14:22:11.090
  ch_7741  succeeded  14:22:12.402
answerKey.symptom: A customer was charged twice for one order. Our logs show one order created.
answerKey.rootCause: The first charge succeeded at the gateway but the response timed out, and the retry carried no idempotency key so the gateway treated it as a new payment.
acceptableFixes: Send a stable idempotency key generated once before the first attempt
Reconcile against the gateway before retrying an ambiguous failure

goodAnswerSignals: Identifies the successful-but-timed-out first charge
Names the missing idempotency key
followUpPrompts: Where must that key be generated for this to work?
mayaPushbacks: Did the first charge actually fail?
